newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan still optimistic on economy despite slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Japan still optimistic on economy despite slowdown.

text.p: The Japanese government remains guardedly optimistic in its view of the economy, saying in a monthly report on Tuesday the economy is recovering despite a temporary slowdown caused by a sales tax rise in April.
However, it said the lingering effects of the tax increase, an unusually cool summer, and fiscal tightening were making it difficult to predict a clear course for the economy.
The Economic Planning Agency's (EPA) report said the economy was continuing to recover but the pace of the recovery was slowing temporarily.
It said housing construction was weak in June after a sustained period of high levels of construction. New car sales in July fell 11.4 percent from a year earlier.
The agency also announced that Japan's household spending, a major barometer for private consumption, fell 4.7 percent in June from a year earlier, partly due to bad weather.
Private economists said the economy was currently weaker than they had expected earlier this year.
EPA Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya said: "Once negative effects of the sales tax hike are out of the way, we can expect the economy to get back on a firm recovery track."
However, another EPA official admitted the sales tax increase was having an unexpectedly prolonged negative effect on consumption.
"We thought the negative impact would disappear in the April-June period, so we still need to see when such effects will vanish," he said.
Private economists do not expect the economy to shrink in the near future, but neither do they expect it to pick up speed.
The economy has been slowly recovering since late 1993, after the late-1980s collapse of the "bubble" economy of inflated asset prices, but it has failed to gather momentum.
"The government view on the economy may be too optimistic," said Tetsuro Sawano, an economist at the Nikko Research Center.
"We cannot expect private consumption to recover to a level seen before the sales tax increase."
The sales tax was increased from three percent to five percent on April 1.
Nikko expects Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by 1.4 percent in the current fiscal year to March 31, 1998, compared with the government's official forecast of 1.9 percent.

Sawano said fiscal tightening characterised by the rise in the sales tax and discontinuation of a special income tax cut was expected to result in a total loss of about seven trillion yen ($59 billion) in people's income this year.
"It would be wrong to predict brisk private consumption this fiscal year," Sawano said.
Jason James, strategist at HSBC James Capel Japan Ltd, said bad weather could push down Japan's GDP by 0.3 percentage points this fiscal year.
"There have been quite a number of typhoons and rainy weather which typically cause weaker consumption," he said.
EPA's Nukaya said the EPA's view was that the economy would pick up in the latter half of the fiscal year.
"Basically, the Japanese economy is becoming firmer, heading for a self-sustainable recovery," he said. ($1=118 yen)
